en: The Fifty Jātaka Stories,
Chapter on Niḷinikā.
3. The Mahābodhi Jātaka:
“What is this staff? What is this antelope skin?
What is this parasol? What are these sandals?”
O Brahmin, why were you hurrying along with your staff, bowl,
and outer robe?
“Which direction do you desire?
“For twelve years I have lived in your presence.”
I do not recall ever hearing the cry of a tawny monkey; this one,
being intoxicated, is merely braying.
“Having heard you, my husband, together with your wife, showing white teeth and baring your fangs, I have lost my faith.”
“Indeed, no fault has been committed here,
as you speak, O brahmin;
rather, I am all the more pleased.”
“Dwell, O Brahmin, do not come!
“In former times he was all-white,
and even more so, he was all-powerful.”
Now the time has come for me to depart, all red with blood;
formerly it was within [the city].
Then in the middle, then outside; before it is swept away,
I shall depart by myself.
One should not associate with one who lacks faith,
even as one might a well with turbid water,
even if one were to dig it up.
Water that smells of mud—
One should resort only to what is clear and avoid what is turbid.
One who needs water should attend upon one who is clear,
just as one seeks a lake;
one should associate with a person who associates with others.
One should not harm one who does not harm;
he who harms one who does not harm follows the way of the unworthy person.
He who does not associate with one who associates,
nor serve one who serves him,
is indeed the most wicked among men.
Like a deer resting on a branch;
through excessive frequent association and through lack of meeting together.
By this, friendships wither through begging at the wrong time;
therefore, one should not go [to a benefactor] constantly.
One should not go too often, nor wait too long;
one should beg at the proper time,
and thus friends do not grow weary.
Through dwelling together for too long,
one who was dear becomes not dear;
let us take our leave of you and go.
"Formerly, the oblations were dear to you.
"If, even while they are thus entreating you with palms joined, you do not understand [the gesture]..."
You do not follow the words of the hundreds of attendants;
thus we entreat you.
“Then you may employ further means.
“If we dwell in this way,
no obstacle shall arise.”
Whether it be for you, O Great King,
or for me, O Increaser of the Realm,
may we indeed behold [the Buddha].
With the passing of days and nights,
if there is an utterance through association,
it conforms to its underlying state.
Whether unwillingly or not, one performs what should not be done,
or even does what should be done; when that which should not be done is performed unwillingly, [one is still stained].
How is one not smeared by evil?
If that matter is both righteous and virtuous,
it is auspicious and not evil.
If your word is true, sir,
then the monkey has indeed been well-slain by me;
for if [it were otherwise] regarding your own doctrine...
One should recognize one's own transgression; you should not reproach me, for such is your doctrine.
If the Lord of the entire world were to determine one’s lifespan,
as well as one’s psychic power and one’s state of misfortune—
Whether the action be good or evil,
the person who performs it is the master; by that, he is defiled.
If it is meaningful and in accordance with the Dhamma,
if it is auspicious and not evil,
and if your word is true—
The monkey has been well-slain by me;
for if he were to recognize the fault in his own argument, [he would have been spared].
"You should not reproach me,
for your own doctrine is such as this:
'If [suffering] is caused by what was done in the past...'"
One encounters pleasure and pain;
one is released from that ancient evil as if from a debt.
The ancient ones were liberated;
how could one here be defiled by evil? If that is both the goal and the Dhamma, [then why this hesitation]?
It is neither good nor evil;
if the word of your honor is true,
then the monkey has been well-slain by me.
If you were to recognize the fault in your own argument, you would not reproach me.
For such indeed is your doctrine:
"The form of living beings arises depending solely upon the four [great elements]."
And wherever form arises,
right there it passes away;
it is only here that a living being lives.
Perishing again and again after death,
this world is annihilated—
both the fools and the wise alike.
When the world is being destroyed,
who here is stained by evil?
If that [world] were both purposeful and righteous, [who would be stained]?
It is neither good nor evil;
if the word of your lord is true,
then the monkey has been well-slain by me.
If you were to recognize the fault in your own argument, you would not reproach me.
For such indeed is your doctrine.
In this world, those who know the kṣatriya class say that fools consider themselves wise men.
One might kill one’s mother and father,
and even one’s eldest brother;
one might kill one’s children and wife as well.
If the purpose were such that one might sit or lie down in the shade of a tree—
One should not break its branch,
for a malicious betrayer of friends is evil.
Then, when an occasion arises...
I shall pull him out by the roots;
even with my whole army, my purpose is served,
for the monkey has been well-slain by me.
If it is meaningful and in accordance with the Dhamma,
if it is auspicious and not evil,
and if the word of the Venerable One is true—
"The monkey has been well-slain by me;
for had he recognized the fault in his own argument,"
You should not reproach me,
for such is your own doctrine;
you are a man who propounds the theory of no-cause.
The one who holds to the doctrine of a creator god, the fatalist, the nihilist,
and the man who relies on the power of the warrior caste.
These are the ignoble persons in the world,
fools who imagine themselves wise;
such a one would commit evil.
Furthermore, one should avoid others as well;
association with bad persons ends in suffering and yields bitter fruit.
In former times, you were a goat,
unafraid as you entered the flock of goats;
having killed a she-goat, a ewe, and a male goat, you were born again.
Having terrified them, such ascetics and brahmins depart wherever they please;
having created a facade, they deceive human beings.
Fasting, sleeping on the bare ground,
dust and dirt, the exertion of the crouching posture,
and eating at irregular intervals and abstaining from drinks—
Those of evil conduct who claim to be arahants—
these are ignoble persons in the world,
fools who imagine themselves to be wise.
Such a person would commit evil,
and furthermore cause others to do so as well;
this is association with the unvirtuous.
The end of suffering is the bitter outcome for those who say "there is no energy" and who proclaim that there is no cause.
Those who praise equally the works of others and their own works, though they are empty—
these are the ignoble persons in the world.
Fools who imagine themselves wise may commit evil deeds, and furthermore,
cause others to do so as well.
Association with those who are not true men ends in suffering and yields bitter fruit;
for if one lacks energy, [it leads to ruin].
Whether an action be wholesome or evil,
a king does not support a carpenter,
nor does he cause him to fashion machines.
And because there is energy,
there is action— both wholesome and evil;
therefore, one causes machines to be made.
The king summons the carpenter:
"If for a hundred years the rain-god does not rain and no snow falls,"
This world would be cut off,
this generation would perish,
were it not for the rain that falls from the sky.
And it causes the snow to melt;
therefore the crops ripen,
and the kingdom is protected for a long time.
If, among cattle crossing over,
the lead bull goes astray,
they all go astray.
When one has gone straight and upright,
even so among humans,
he who is considered the best—
If he practices what is unrighteous,
how much more so the rest of the people;
the entire kingdom lies in suffering.
If the king is unrighteous,
yet the bull goes straight when the cattle are crossing, [the herd will follow him].
All the cows go straight when the leader has gone straight;
even so among human beings...
If he who is esteemed as the best practices the Dhamma,
how much more so should the rest of the people?
The whole country dwells in happiness if the king is righteous,
just as [all parts of] a large, fruit-bearing tree [prosper].
He who cuts the fruit while it is unripe does not know its flavor,
and his seed is destroyed.
A kingdom ruled by unrighteousness is like a great tree;
it does not even know its own essence.
And his kingdom perishes—
he who plucks the ripe fruit from a great, fruit-bearing tree.
He discerns its sap,
yet its seed does not perish;
such is the kingdom, comparable to a great tree.
He who rules according to the Dhamma perceives the true flavor [of sovereignty],
and his kingdom does not perish.
And that king who rules his realm by unrighteousness,
though he may possess all medicinal herbs, that king—
A Kshatriya becomes an adversary;
likewise, he harms the merchants who are engaged in buying and selling.
In the offering of the strength-giving oblation,
he is obstructed by his treasury;
[he is] one who knows the excellent field for the strike.
In battle, when the enemy has been defeated and the king is exalted,
he becomes arrogant and oppresses with his power.
In that same way, the seers who are self-restrained and live the holy life do not harm;
whereas a kshatriya who acts contrary to the Dharma [does].
He is obstructed by hell.
And that king who stands on unrighteousness,
who kills his innocent wife—
One who is cruel brings about trouble and is obstructed by his own children; therefore,
one should practice righteousness toward the people of the land.
One should not harm cattle, nor strength,
nor sages; one should conduct oneself equally toward one's children and wife.
Such was that lord of the earth,
Raṭṭhapāla, free from anger;
yet he caused his very enemies to tremble.
“Inda indeed is the lord of the asuras.
Thus ends the third Jātaka, the Mahābodhi-jātaka.
The Fiftieth Chapter (Paṇṇāsa-nipāta) is concluded.
Its summary verse:
The first is called Saniḷīnika-avhayana;
the second, however, is Saummadantivara.
But the third was named Bodhisiri;
these three were declared by the Conqueror to be beautiful.
